div.p: A majority of multi-rate real-time systems are constrained by a multitude of timing requirements, in addition to the traditional deadlines on well-studied response times. This means, the timing predictability of these systems not only depends on the schedulability of certain task sets but also on the timely propagation of data through the chains of tasks from sensors to actuators. In the automotive industry, four different timing constraints corresponding to various data propagation delays are commonly specified on the systems. This paper identifies and addresses the source of pessimism as well as optimism in the calculations for one such delay, namely the reaction delay, in the state-of-the-art analysis that is already implemented in several industrial tools. Furthermore, a generic framework is proposed to compute all the four end-to-end data propagation delays, complying with the established delay semantics, in a scheduler and hardware-agnostic manner. This allows analysis of the system models already at early development phases, where limited system information is present. The paper further introduces mechanisms to generate job-level dependencies, a partial ordering of jobs, which need to be satisfied by any execution platform in order to meet the data propagation timing requirements. The job-level dependencies are first added to all task chains of the system and then reduced to its minimum required set such that the job order is not affected. Moreover, a necessary schedulability test is provided, allowing for varying the number of CPUs. The experimental evaluations demonstrate the tightness in the reaction delay with the proposed framework as compared to the existing state-of-the-art and practice solutions.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: With evolving system complexity, the notion of correctness in most real-time systems is no longer confined to guaranteeing individual independent task response times in isolation, but rather meeting timing constraints on the data propagation across a semantically related chain of tasks. This could typically manifest itself as reading one or more sensor values, fusing and consuming the gathered information in a meaningful manner by possibly multiple control tasks and finally actuating the desired behavior within predefined time bounds. Further, complex applications are, in general, designed using multi-rate task chains [1], [2], where tasks within a chain can be activated with different periods independent of each other. This could lead to undersampling and oversampling effects where, assuming that task chains are composed of consecutive producer-consumer segments, the consumer either samples data faster or slower than the producer task can generate it. These effects lead to data being either overwritten or lost depending on the (numerous possible) data propagation across the chain. Hence the timing analysis of data propagation delays is crucial, yet non-trivial under these circumstances.

Apart from the aforementioned problems arising out of "multi-rate" tasks, this delay analysis is influenced by other fundamental aspects like the scheduling algorithm deployed and the underlying hardware characteristics. However, the software in these systems, especially in the automotive domain, is too complex to be developed by one supplier. Hence, software development generally follows the distributed concurrent engineering paradigm [3]. Integration occurs much later at the OEM-end and hence while designing the software, information regarding the target architecture and/or the target scheduling algorithm or the co-running applications is typically not known at early design phases. Hence, designers need to master the art of building composable systems in the face of uncertainty and limited information.

A case in point is that automotive applications [2], [4], [5] for example, need to be verified at design time itself. However the majority of commercially available state-of-thepractice tools found in the industry [6], [7], [8], [9], [10], can be only applied closer to the implementation phases since they require a complete definition of the system together with implementation-level details [11], and thus are not suitable for early timing analysis. Another existing lacuna in these implementations comes from the analysis engines [11] implemented in these tools, which lead to incorrect estimates, when calculating one important variant of data propagation delay (reaction delay) as is identified in this work.

Alternatively, authors in [12] propose a method that analyzes event chains in a hardware-agnostic manner and are thus congenial for early design phase analysis. However, the applied method can only handle one of the data propagation delay semantics (data age) and is thus limited in applicability, given that systems, in accordance to their functionality may need to conform to the age delay as well as several other delay semantics.

In this work, we propose to mitigate these deficiencies by presenting a generic framework to calculate general data propagation delays agnostic of the hardware or scheduler employed. This allows to decide already early-on if the specified data propagation delay constraints in a system of tasks with

possibly different delay semantics can be realized or not. The concept of job-level dependencies is utilized to introduce a necessary partial ordering on the jobs that are involved in the specified data propagation delay constraints. The contributions can be summarized as follows:
• We identify and highlight the shortcomings of the current reaction delay computations and propose a revised safe computation.

• We propose a generic framework to compute data propagation delays for the established delay semantics in a scheduler agnostic manner, enabling its usage during early design phases. • For cases where unconstrained execution leads to missed data propagation deadlines, we propose enforcing joblevel dependencies to the corresponding event chains. • In order to avoid over-constraining the system we optimize the number of job-level dependencies, without impacting the systems' performance/ behavior while also reducing the constraints that must be applied in the implementation phase. • We then present a necessary schedulability test to validate the application of the proposed job-level dependencies towards reducing data propagation delays. • The effect of the revised calculations on the reaction delay is demonstrated by experiments. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. In Section II the related work is discussed. Section III introduces the required background information, and Section IV revisits and revises existing work. In Section V it is shown how to compute data propagation paths for all data propagation delay constraints, followed by Section VI where it is shown how job-level dependencies can be specified on the system to meet data propagation delay constraints. Section VII provides a method to prune job-level dependencies. Section VIII presents a necessary schedulability test. Evaluations are presented in Section IX, and finally, in Section X conclusions are drawn.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: Guaranteeing the schedulability of real-time systems is crucial to satisfy the tasks' local deadlines. Since the seminal work of Liu and Layland [13] for hard real-time scheduling algorithms, and Josephs and Pandya [14] for response-time analysis, much research has been conducted to guarantee the tasks' local properties on single [15], [16] and multiprocessor [17] platforms.

On the other hand, the complexity of today's systems requires additional timing constraints on the data propagation through a chain of tasks in order to fulfill the system requirements. In the automotive industry, such a timing model is defined by the TIMMO-2-USE [18] project which resulted in the Timing Architecture Description Language (TADL2) [19]. This language is used to describe timing constraints in EAST-ADL [5] and AUTOSAR [20]. EAST-ADL is an Architecture Description Language (ADL) designed to cover the complete automotive design process from the vehicle level to the implementation level, while AUTOSAR focuses on the implementation level.

Several communication forms among tasks can be found in different system areas. Register communication is typically implemented in automotive systems [2], where data can be overwritten or consumed multiple times, depending on the activation periods of the producer and consumer tasks. In contrast, the work in [21] and [22] target the end-to-end delay 1analysis of the systems with causal data communication, i.e. a receiving task cannot be executed unless all its input data have arrived. The Logical Execution Time (LET) paradigm is gaining attention in the automotive industry [23]. The LET paradigm was introduced with the time-triggered programing language Giotto [24], [25]. This paradigm effectively decouples communication from task execution, which greatly simplifies the analysis of data propagation delays [26] but may result in larger data propagation delays [27].

The analysis of data propagation delays in multi-rate systems where register communication is applied was first proposed in [11]. Rajeev et al. [28] compute data propagation delays using a model-checking based technique, and Mubeen et al. [10] discuss the implementation of data propagation delay analysis in an industrial tool suite. The data propagation delay analysis is adopted by the industry and available in several commercial tools [6], [7], [9], [8]. However, all of these techniques are applicable only at the implementation level, where response times of tasks can be obtained.

In [12], it is shown how to obtain upper bounds on the data propagation delays at higher abstraction levels with respect to the implementation level. This work, however, only focuses on the maximum data age, one of the data propagation delay semantics defined in [19], [5], [20]. This analysis method is implemented in MECHAniSer [29] which is an academic tool 2 .

In addition to the analysis of data propagation delays, several works focus on the synthesis of task activation periods [30], [31] in order to satisfy specified data propagation delay constraints. In [12], a heuristic solution is presented to augment a task set with dependencies on the execution order of individual jobs, so-called job-level dependencies, in order to satisfy the specified data age constraints. In this work, we focus on the analysis at design time and synthesis of job-level dependencies. Thus, the execution of the systems is out of the scope of this work. This is for example addressed in [32], [33], [34], [35] for fixed-and dynamic-priority systems and singleand multi-core platforms. Scheduling of tasks that are subject of precedence constraints is discussed in [36]. The offsets and deadlines of the tasks that are constrained by precedence constraints are adjusted such that the tasks can be scheduled with Earliest Deadline First (EDF).

Our method is different from the existing approaches by taking all possible data propagation delay semantics into account when analyzing systems at higher abstraction levels. We then show how to augment such systems with necessary job-level dependencies such that the specified constraints are met and later show how to reduce this set without changing the imposed execution order of jobs. Finally, a necessary schedulability test for multiprocessor systems is presented

div.head: III. BACKGROUND AND SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: This section first introduces the application model and then discusses the different important aspects of data propagation delays.

div.head: A. Application Model
div.p: We assume that an application consists of a set of periodic tasks Γ. Each task τ i ∈ Γ can be characterized by the tuple {C i , T i }, where C i denotes the task's Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET), and T i denotes its activation period. The WCET of a task can either be specified as execution time constraint in early design phases [19], [5], [20], or as result of static timing analysis [37], if detailed system information is present. It is further assumed that tasks have implicit deadlines, i.e. the deadline is equal to the period. In the remainder of the paper all data propagation delay calculations assume tasks to execute within their local timing constraints, i.e. it is assumed that the task set is schedulable. To ease the presentation the release time and deadline of the j th job of τ i is represented as R i,j and D i,j respectively. Without loss of generality, all tasks are released at the same time (i.e., there are no offsets). A target platform for such an application is a multicore processor. Tasks in the system communicate using register-based communication, as it is commonly used in industrial systems [2]. In this communication, tasks communicate via shared registers. This means, a sending task writes the value to the shared register, and a receiving task reads the value from the register. This has the advantage that there is no need for signaling between the two tasks and the last-is-best semantic holds.

Cause-Effect Chain: A cause-effect chain defines a logical relation for the data propagation between a sequence of tasks, where the main interest lies in the delay a certain input value faces until the corresponding response becomes available at the end of the cause-effect chain.

A cause-effect chain is represented by the Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) denoted by ζ. The DAG ζ contains the set of nodes V, and the set of edges E. There is no restriction on the activation periods of tasks in a chain. This means, a single cause-effect chain can contain arbitrary periods which may lead to over-and under-sampling between these tasks. A single cause-effect chain can further have fork and join operations, but the initial and final nodes need to be the same for all paths. To simplify the presentation in the rest of the paper, only sequential cause-effect chains are examined. This is however not a limitation, since a cause-effect chain that includes fork/join operations can be represented by several sequential cause-effect chains. Each cause-effect chain ζ can have a specified data propagation delay constraint. This means, the temporal behavior of the chain is constrained by the specified timing constraint corresponding to the concrete semantic of the data propagation delay.

div.head: B. Data Propagation Delay Semantics
div.p: This paper considers the data propagation delay semantics that are defined in AUTOSAR [20], as well as in EAST-ADL [5], and TADL2 [19]. Fig. 1 presents a scenario containing three different tasks, that execute at different activation periods. The tasks define a cause-effect chain in the order τ A → τ B → τ C . τ A has the slowest activation rate with a period of 8-time units. τ B executes with a period of 2-time units, and τ C with a period of 4-time units. Thus, this example constitutes a multi-rate chain, where oversampling (i.e., the consumer is activated at a faster rate than the producer) is observed between τ A and τ B , and undersampling (i.e., the producer is activated at a faster rate than the consumer) can be observed between τ B and τ C . The data propagation between instances of consecutive tasks in the chain is visualized via dashed arrows. The propagation from an instance that produces data that is never consumed is depicted by a dashed line that ends without an arrow head. Each path that can be reached from an instance of the initial task of the chain up to an instance of the last task in the chain is referred to as a complete path. Four different data propagation delay semantics can be observed for a multi-rate chain [11], which can be defined in the following.

1) Last to Last (Data Age): The data age is defined as the maximum time between the output of a cause-effect chain and the corresponding input, where the output and input must be causally related. Thus, the elapsed time is perceived from the response of the chain until the sampling time of the corresponding data at the beginning of the chain. This can be represented by looking at the availability of input data, from the last time an input event can be recognized, i.e. the time the task is sampling the data until the time this data has the last effect on the output. This semantic can thus be defined as last to last, ∆ LtoL or respectively ∆ Age .

2) Last to First: The last to first semantic, ∆ LtoF , can be constructed by considering the time it takes for the data to propagate to the end of the chain over the first complete path after sampling by a job of the first task in the chain.

3) First to First (Reaction Delay): The reaction delay is the inverse of the data age. Here the maximum time between the arrival of a stimulus event at the beginning of a causeeffect chain and the first response at the end of the chain is of importance. It is important that there is a causal relationship between the event and the generated response. The first time an arriving stimulus event can have an impact is right after the sampling of the successor instance. For example in Fig. 1, the first event arrives just after the first instance reads its input τ 1 , then the event is only read by the second instance of τ 1 . This semantic is thus named as first to first, ∆ F toF or respectively ∆ Reaction . This delay type always has a ∆ LtoF component, and thus ∆ LtoF < ∆ F toF .
4) First to Last: Finally, the first to last semantic, ∆ F toL , can be defined as the time from the earliest stimulus event until the latest effect of this data at the end of the chain.

div.head: C. Data Propagation Tree
div.p: A Data Propagation Tree (DPT) is a representation of all possible communication scenarios among different jobs of the tasks that are part of a cause-effect chain, agnostic to scheduling and hardware, and was first introduced in [12]. Given a cause-effect chain ζ, the DPT includes information for the possible data propagation between the different jobs of the involved tasks τ i ∈ V, agnostic to the scheduling. This means, if there exists a scenario where two jobs may exchange data, an edge is present in the DPT. A DPT is defined as T = {J , P}, where J is the set of jobs that propagate the data, and P is the set of edges that mark a possible data propagation. Note that edges are only possible between jobs of tasks that are adjacent in ζ, and they are directed from the producer task's job to the consumer task's job.

Given the characteristics of a cause-effect chain, one DPT exists for each initial job of the cause-effect chain. Initial jobs are all jobs of the first task in the cause-effect chain that need to be executed within the hyperperiod of the cause-effect chain. Given that new data is introduced into the system at these points, a DPT is computed.

A path from an initial node to a node of the last task in the cause-effect chain is called Data Propagation Path. Hence, it contains all jobs the data propagates through, if this scenario is observed during runtime.

In [12] it is shown that the maximum data age, or ∆ LtoL , is upper bounded by the maximum distance between the release of an initial job R Start in a DPT, and the deadline of the last job in the path D End .

div.head: D. Job-Level Dependency
div.p: A job-level dependency is a constraint on the execution order of the jobs of two tasks. Such a constraint is intended to add determinism to the data communication in a multi-rate system and was first introduced in the synchronous language PRELUDE [32].
We define a job-level dependency as τ A (i,j)

---→ τ B . The dependency constrains the execution order of jobs of τ A and τ B . Since the two tasks may execute at different rates, i.e. periods, the index of the constrained jobs is shown above the arrow operator. In the example, the i th job of τ A must be executed before the j th job of τ B . The indexes always refer to the jobs within the hyperperiod of the constrained tasks, i.e. LCM (T A , T B ) and repeat afterwards.

div.head: IV. SAFE AND TIGHT DATA PROPAGATION DELAY CALCULATIONS FOR REACTION DELAY
div.p: Calculating safe and tight estimates on the data propagation delays is of great importance for automotive systems as they are often subject to strict timing constraints. The current state of the art regarding the data propagation timing analysis is presented in [11]. As mentioned earlier, this analysis has been implemented in several tools. We identify that if a cause-effect chain experiences an undersampling relationship between two tasks, the provided bounds in [11] for the maximum reaction delay may lead to unsafe estimates.

div.head: A. Identified Source of Optimism and Pessimism in the Calculations for Reaction Delay
div.p: This subsection identifies the unsafe scenarios in the calculations for the reaction delay. In [11] the calculations for the reaction delay are constituted by the ∆ LtoF , plus an additional delay that is defined as the input sampling delay ∆ Input . This input sampling delay needs to be appended to ∆ LtoF since trigger events can arrive asynchronously at any time at the beginning of the chain. In [11] it is reasoned, that the time that needs to be taken into account for ∆ Input is the maximum time between two instances of the first task in the chain that has at least one complete path. The reasoning being that the first instance of the first task just missed the event, so it is picked up by the next instance of the first task that results in a complete path along the chain. This assumption may lead to optimistic and pessimistic results under register based communication, given the definition of reaction delay as presented in Section III-B3.

Fig. 2 demonstrates the concept of ∆ input . The execution trace of three tasks is shown, τ 1 to τ 3 . This trace is generated by the state-of-the-practice tool Rubus-ICE [6]. These tasks constitute a multi-rate effect chain, since τ 2 is activated with a slower period than τ 1 , and τ 3 with a slower activation period than τ 2 . Fig. 2 further shows the earliest input events, that are observed just after the previous instance of τ 1 is scheduled. The data paths between the instances of the tasks are further shown, which visualize the challenge of multi-rate systems.

In the undersampling situation, i.e. the consumer is activated with a lower period than the producer, certain input values need to be skipped as a result of the period selection. This can be seen by the data paths that result from the third and fourth instances of τ 1 that produce data which are overwritten before τ 2 can consume them.

Fig. 2 visualizes the suggested input interval of [11] as the time between the activation of the two jobs of the first task of the cause-effect chain that result in a complete path (from the second instance of τ 1 to the fifth instance of τ 1 , that result in outputs A and D, respectively). We further visualize the computed maximum reaction delay by the state-of-the-practice tool suite which implements the analysis of [11]. According to the definition of the reaction delay [20], [5], [19], the time of the first causally related response of the effect-chain to an input event is constrained. This is, however, not given using the shown input interval, as can be seen with the input events B and C, that never reach the end of the chain, these events have an infinite reaction delay as per definition. As an input that was consumed by such an instance never reaches the end of the cause-effect chain for some propagation paths, the computed result is optimistic and unsafe for these paths. On the other hand, the input interval yields pessimistic results for the reaction delay of paths that reach the end of the causeeffect chain, as here the period of the first task of the causeeffect chain limits the length of ∆ input in the same way it does for single-rate systems [38]. In Fig. 2 we illustrate the reaction delay as computed by [11]. However, the actual reaction delay is upper bounded by the path D, as any earlier event would have been consumed by the fourth instance of τ 1 .

div.head: B. Proposed Solution to Reduce Pessimism in Reaction Delay
div.p: The source of pessimism in the reaction delay comes from the calculations of the input interval in the existing analysis [11]. In order to compute safe and tight reaction delay estimates, we adjust the calculations of the input interval. Hence, we remove the pessimism in the calculations without fundamentally altering the established way of computing the reaction delay in [11]. It is first important to redefine the safe input interval bounds, which is an extension of the period of the first task of the chain. We propose that the input interval can safely and tightly computed when bounded as follows.

Lemma 1: A safe interval is defined as the maximum time from the occurrence of an input event until being sampled by an instance of the first task in the chain. This interval is bounded by the maximum distance between two consecutive jobs of the first task in the cause-effect chain.

Proof 1: This can be shown by contradiction. Assume the interval between two events spans from an instance τ i,j to an instance τ i,j+2 . This would mean that an event which arrives just after τ i,j starts its execution can be recognized by τ i,j+2 . The contradiction directly follows the register communications properties, i.e. a later instance of the same task will overwrite the data that is produced by an earlier instance, irrespective of the state of other tasks in the system. Since τ i,j+1 needs to execute before τ i,j+2 , it is τ i,j+1 that consumes the event. Thus, once τ i,j+2 reads the input values the event is not pending anymore and the event is never propagated to the end of the cause-effect chain. Fig. 2: Execution trace of the task set generated by Rubus ICE [6]. The worstcase reaction delay that is identified by the analysis engine [11], [10], as well as the different observed data paths, are visualized.

Lemma 1, together with the observation that ∆ Input only includes the time up to the release of the consuming job, ∆ Input can be upper bounded by one period of the first task in the cause-effect chain.

div.head: C. Effective Input Period of the Chain
div.p: The revised calculations for the reaction delay highlight certain challenges for the system designer. When task parameters are chosen, this typically is done in accordance with the physical constraints of the system. For example, a sensor value must be read frequently enough to detect all its information. When considering the complete cause-effect chain, over-and under-sampling results in data either being lost or duplicated, possibly in each segment of the chain. This can lead to different behavior than expected. We illustrate this scenario with the example of Fig. 2. The input signals A to D are read by τ 1 every 6 time units. However, the involved periods of the cause-effect chain lead to loss of data of inputs B and C. Consequently, while τ 1 reads every 6-time units, only the data that is read at t = 6 and t = 24 reaches the end of the chain, whereas the data which is read at t = 12 and t = 18 never produce any effect on the output. Thus, two consecutive instances of τ 1 read values that impact the system, followed by two consecutive instances that do not.

Let us assume the physical input that needs to be observed is a sine signal, as shown in Fig. 3. This signal has a frequency of f = 1/24 and is periodically read by τ 1 . Since τ 1 executes with an activation period of t = 6, the sine signal is read with Fig. 3: Trace of a sinus signal, representing the physical input. time instances at which the effect chain of Fig. 2 reads its input values, and the corresponding times the chain produces its outputs.

4 times its frequency. Fig. 3 depicts these reading points by green and red colored arrows that represent instances of τ 1 that are connected to valid (green) and incomplete data paths (red). The same figure also visualizes the time instances for which the corresponding output becomes available at the end of the chain, and the value of the corresponding input signal.

As can be seen, the complete information of the input signal is lost due to the characteristics of the chain, even though the rate at which τ 1 reads the sine signal is sufficiently fast. Thus, while the period of the first task in a cause-effect chain may be chosen according to the signal that needs to be observed, the over-and under-sampling within a causeeffect chain can lead to a different behavior than expected. It is evident from Fig. 3 that the effective input period of a chain can be different from the period of the first task in the cause-effect chain. In order to design the system such that all input events are detected, the system designer needs to take the effective input period of the chain into account. Since scheduling can affect the execution order of jobs, a safe effective period (i.e. the periodicity that actually effects the output) for a cause-effect chain should be determined before the detailed information about the scheduler is available.

The effective input period is limited on one side by the task of the chain that has the largest period, but on the other side also by the concrete scheduling decisions. For a causeeffect chain ζ with known schedule, the effective input period T ζ can be obtained by taking the maximum distance between two complete paths. E.g., for example ∆ Input shown in Fig. 2. Note that this is equivalent to the original input delay of [11]. The solutions proposed in this section are incorporated in the calculations for the reaction delay at higher abstraction levels presented in the next section.

div.head: V. ADDRESSING GENERAL DATA PROPAGATION DELAYS
div.p: This section introduces the calculation for data propagation delays for all the established delay semantics. The calculations are based on the concept of data propagation tree which represents all possible data paths that may be observed during the system execution. We identify paths of that tree and show that they link to upper bounds for the different data propagation delay semantics. This then allows to determine bounds on the data propagation delay semantics already during system design.

div.head: A. Different Regions of the Data Propagation Tree
div.p: The DPT reflects all possible behaviors of the data propagation for one cause-effect chain. While the data age is affected by the data propagation path with the longest data age, for the reaction constraint it is of interest when the data first reaches the output. During runtime, several paths may be never reached due to the characteristics of the applied scheduling algorithm. This also includes paths to early instances of the last task in the cause-effect chain. Thus, to predict the worstcase for the reaction delay it is important to know which data propagation path will definitely be reached given the task set characteristics. Such a path is called necessary data propagation path (NDPP). In the following section it is shown how the NDPP can be calculated based on the DPT and the task set.

div.head: B. Calculating the Necessary Data Propagation Path
div.p: The necessary data-propagation path can be found by examining the condition for a necessary propagation of data between two tasks. For this to happen, a job of a successor task must be released no later than the deadline of the predecessor task's job. Let us denote by S k NJ,i,j , the set of jobs of τ k that necessarily consume the data of τ i,j or of a later instance of τ i .
div.formula: S k NJ,i,j = {τ k,l |R k,l ≥ Di,j}(2)
div.p: Fig. 4 illustrates this at the example of a chain containing only two tasks. Lemma 2: A path between τ i,j to τ k,l constitutes a necessary data path , where R k,l = min τ k,x ∈S k NJ,i,j R k,x . Proof 2: This can be proven by contradiction. It is first shown that it cannot be an earlier instance of τ k,l : This follows from the communication semantic and Eq. 2. An earlier instance, say τ k,l-1 is released before the deadline of τ i,j . This means, if τ i,j finishes its execution within its deadline and τ k,l-1 starts its execution when it is released, τ k,l-1 reads the data that is produced by τ i,j-1 since τ i,j writes its output at a later time. It can easily be seen that a later instance of τ k,l cannot be part of the necessary path as the jobs of τ k are released sequentially in time.

The complete path from the first task's job until the job of the last task in the effect chain can then easily be computed in a recursive manner. Note that this path is always a path of the general data-propagation tree.

div.head: C. Timing Estimates for all Data Propagation Delay Semantics
div.p: The NDPP is a key abstraction which facilitates the computation of the data propagation delays, considering the different semantics. The delay ∆ LtoF can be computed by looking at the start and end nodes of the NDPP, i.e. in the DPT of Fig. 4 from the start node τ 1,1 to the end node τ 2,5 . If intermediate nodes are resent, they don't need to be considered as the DPT already guarantees that the propagation of data on this path is possible. If the first job in this path starts its execution directly at release time, and the last job of the path just finishes within its deadline, the maximum delay is reached:
The reaction delay, or ∆ F toF can now easily be obtained by adding the input sampling delay to ∆ LtoF :

In the section above, we described how we can compute the data propagation delays purely based on the DPT, and thus without detailed system information verify if a given constraint is met. In the next section, we address the case wherein a specified delay constraint is not met.

div.head: VI. SPECIFYING JOB-LEVEL DEPENDENCIES TO MEET
div.p: THE DATA PROPAGATION DELAY CONSTRAINTS It is crucial to identify if the data propagation delays cannot be met and mitigate the problem by enforcing certain execution order constraints in the form of job-level dependencies. Such measures enable a correct-by-construction approach and thereby costly retro-corrections at the later phases are avoided. In this section, we propose how to specify the appropriate job-level dependencies to ensure that the specified timing constraints are met.

div.head: A. Job-Level Dependencies to Meet the Reaction Delay Constraint
div.p: Addressing multi-rate effect chains with specified reaction constraints can be accomplished by taking the characteristics of the constraint type into account. For the reaction constraint, the first appearance of the input data at the output of the chain is of importance. Further, this delay is essentially the sum of two delays that can be observed in the system, the input delay and the Last to First delay:

The input delay cannot be influenced by the job-level dependencies since it is dependent on the period of the first task in the chain. On the other hand, ∆ LtoF can be influenced -this means, we can determine an upper bound for ∆ LtoF such that the specified reaction constraint is met:

In order to meet the reaction constraint, all initial jobs of the cause-effect chain need to meet the requirement. This means, a data path of each of the DPT needs to exist that experiences a maximum delay of ∆ LtoF . Each DPT can be addressed separately.

For a single DPT, the job of the last task in the chain that needs to carry the data can be determined by considering the job of the first task in the chain, let us say τ i,j , and the last task of the chain, lets say τ k,l .

where τ i,j ∈ DPT and τ k,l ∈ DPT. Since there can be more than one job of τ k that fulfills this requirement we can further restrict the selection by searching the job of τ k that has the largest instance id l and fulfills Equation 8. The job τ i,j is already known since each DPT contains, by definition, only one job of the first task in the chain. Given that the jobs τ i,j and τ k,l are part of the same DPT, we know that there exists at least one data path from τ i,j to τ k,l . As the data path in the tree progresses it could fork into multiple instances; then the path that includes the earlier instance is discarded.
In order to force the data propagation along this specific data path job-level dependencies can be added between all chain segments along this data path, as we will show in the following lemma.

Lemma 3: In a DPT which does not meet a specified reaction constraints, all job-level dependencies on the identified data path in accordance to Equation 8, are necessary in order to meet the reaction constraint.

Proof 3: Assume a system where the job-level dependency τ A (i,j) ---→ τ B is specified. A schedule does not meet the dependency and the data propagates from τ A,i to τ B,j+1 . This directly violates the specified constraint as the data now propagates to a later instance of τ B . This results in a data path that ends in a task instance that does not satisfy Equation 8. This is true for each dependency specified along the chain since none of it can be skipped without violating the system constraints.

div.head: B. Job-Level Dependencies to Meet Data Age Constraints
div.p: Similar to the reaction constraint, the data age constraint can be met by adding job-level dependencies to the system. The data age constraint is concerned when the last output that relates to a certain input sample is produced. If the related data is provided to a later output instance, the constraint is violated.

In [12], a heuristic solution is presented to add such joblevel dependencies in the case of the data age constraint. In contrast, here we show how to specify necessary job-level dependencies to the system.

For each DPT, select the initial node of the tree, say τ i,j . The job of the last task in the cause-effect chain that is reachable over the DPT from τ i,j and satisfies Equation 9 is chosen. If multiple such jobs exist, the one with largest index is of interest as it will be executed last.

In contrast to the reaction delay constraint, with data age it is of interest that the data will not be propagated to a later instance of the last task in the cause-effect chain. The same methodology to assign job-level dependencies as in [12] can be applied. In contrast to [12] where dependencies are assigned heuristically, the dependencies are added to each level of the DPT, without the concern for other system metrics. Later in Section VII it is shown how to minimize the set of specified job-level dependencies without affecting the imposed ordering of the jobs execution order.

VII. PRUNING JOB-LEVEL DEPENDENCIES Given a set of job-level dependencies that are specified for a number of tasks, it is possible to reduce their number, while keeping the same partial ordering of jobs. This is possible by exploiting different characteristics of the system.

div.head: A. Job-Level Dependencies Constrain Same Job Instances
div.p: Assume two tasks, τ A and τ B . Two job-level dependencies are specified: τ A (i,l+j) ----→ τ B and τ A (i+k,l) ----→ τ B (see Fig. 5a).
Fig. 5: Pruning job-level dependencies with shared constrained instances.

Lemma 4: A job-level dependency can be removed from the system without impacting the defined job order, if the joblevel dependencies are defined on the same tasks in the same direction (i.e. from τ A to τ B ), and k ≥ 0 and j ≥ 0.

Proof 4: From the system model it is known that jobs of the same task are executed in sequential manner, where there is an ordering between jobs such that τ A,l is executed before τ A,l+j , where j ∈ N + . Four different cases are examined in order to proof the lemma.
Case 1 (k = 0; j = 0): This case is trivial as the two job-level dependencies are identical and thus either of them can be removed.

Case 2 (k = 0; j > 0): In this case, the two joblevel dependencies origin from the same source node. Since both job-level dependencies have the same successor task, but a different instance, it can directly be followed that the dependency that ends at the job of τ B with larger index can be omitted because of the ordering of jobs of the same task.

Case 3 (k > 0; j = 0): In this case, the two job-level dependencies end in the same instance of the successor task. In such a setting, the job-level dependency that originates from τ A with a smaller instance can be omitted. This can be directly followed from the previously discussed job ordering for the jobs of the same task. Since the job-level dependencies end in the same job, the job-level dependency that starts at an earlier instance of the predecessor task can be omitted without affecting the job ordering.

Case 4 (k > 0; j > 0): In this case, the job-level dependencies cross (as seen in Fig. 5a). The job-level dependency that originates at the instance i of the predecessor task and ends at the instance l + j of the successor task can be omitted without affecting the job ordering since the second job-level dependency causes a later instance of τ A to be executed before an earlier instance of τ B . Thus the job sequence is given even if the job-level dependency is omitted.
Based on the four cases it can be concluded that, if two
Fig. 6: Two task instances that are constrained but do not overlap in their execution.
job-level dependencies interact in the jobs they constrain, one of them can be omitted without affecting the execution order of the jobs.

div.head: B. Execution Intervals do not Overlap
div.p: A job-level dependency is always fulfilled, and hence can be omitted, if the execution interval of the successor job starts after the execution interval of the predecessor job.

Assume two tasks, τ A and τ B , where a job-level dependency τ A (j,i) --→ τ B is specified between them and their release and deadlines are as illustrated in Fig. 6. The job-level dependency is always met and can thus be removed, as shown in the following lemma.
Lemma 5: The job-level dependency τ A (j,i)
div.formula: --→ τ B can be omitted if it holds that T A • j ≤ T B • (i -1).
div.p: Proof 5: This can be shown by considering the predecessor job to finish its execution as late as possible and the successor job to finish its execution as early as possible. If the predecessor job finishes its execution at t 1 = T A • j it finishes with its deadline, i.e., if it finishes later, the tasks local deadline will be missed. On the other hand, the successor job can start its execution as early as t 2 = T B • (i -1), if it starts executing earlier it violates the system model. Hence, if t 1 ≤ t 2 the ordering of the job-level dependency is always given.

div.head: VIII. TESTING SCHEDULABILITY OF THE SYSTEM
div.p: In Section VI it was shown which job-level dependencies need to be present in the system such that all data propagation delay constraints are met. This section presents a necessary schedulability test that indicates already at the design time if a schedule for a set of tasks with an accompanying set of job-level dependencies might be found.

div.head: A. Impact of Job-Level Dependencies on Execution Intervals
div.p: Adding a job-level dependency impacts the possible execution interval of the constrained jobs [12]. If there is a joblevel dependency τ A (j,i) --→ τ B , a precedence relationship exists between job τ B,i and τ A,j . τ B,i cannot start before C A time units after the release of τ A,j (see Fig. 7a). In order to give τ B,i time to execute before its deadline, τ A,j must finish its execution at least C B time units before the deadline of τ B,i (see Fig. 7b).
For a job without any constraints, the execution window is equivalent to [R i,j , D i,j ], where the release of a job τ i,j is
) ",' ( ",' (a) Earliest execution of τ A,j .

) ",' ( ",' (b) Latest execution of τ B,i . Fig. 7: A job-level dependency τ A (j,i) ---→ τ B and its effect on the execution window of the constrained jobs τ A,j and τ B,i . defined as R i,j , and its deadline is defined as D i,j respectively. If job-level dependencies are specified this execution window may get reduced as discussed earlier (see Fig. 7). The modified bounds of the execution window of a job due to specified job-level dependencies are defined as E Start i,j and E End i,j respectively [36].

of the job may get extended if there are job-level dependencies specified that end in the job under question. On the other hand, E End i,j may get reduced if there are job-level dependencies specified that start with the job under question (see Fig. 8). For the scheduler to have a chance to schedule the job, it must hold that:
div.formula: E End i,j -E Start i,j ≥ Ci(10)
div.p: For a necessary schedulability test of the task set under the specified job-level dependencies, it needs to be verified that Equation 10 is satisfied.
We can formulate E Start i,j
and E End i,j

for the general case. Assume the set dep prev (τ i,j ) includes all jobs of tasks ∈ Γ that are constrained with a job-level dependency to be executed before τ i,j . Similarly, the set dep suc (τ i,j ) includes all jobs of tasks ∈ Γ that are constrained with a job-level dependency to be executed after τ i,j This means, dep prev (τ i,j ) affects E Start i,j , and dep suc (τ i,j ) affects E End i,j . Since this test is intended to be used during early design phases it may not be known how many cores area available in the target processor or which scheduling algorithm is applied. Hence, we formulate the problem as a function of the number of cores n, where n is the number of identical cores the target hardware offers. Let θ n prev be the earliest time at which all jobs ∈ dep prev (τ i,j ) had the chance to execute. The new beginning of τ i,j 's execution window can then be computed by:
div.formula: E Start i,j = max(θ n prev , Ri,j)(11)
div.p: Likewise, θ n suc is the latest time by which jobs ∈ dep suc (τ i,j ) need to start executing in order to meet their deadlines. This then allows to compute the end of τ i,j 's execution window:
div.formula: E End i,j = min(θ n suc , Ri,j+1)(12)
div.p: As can be seen, both, θ n prev and θ n suc , are dependent on the number of cores n. Having a larger number of cores allows to schedule the dependent jobs in parallel and hence E Start i,j and E End i,j need to be adjusted less, which then increases the likelihood that Equation 10 is satisfied. In order to determine θ n pred and θ n suc one needs to find the earliest and respectively latest time the dependent jobs finish their execution or need to start their execution.

The general problem can be formulated as to find the minimum point in time θ n where all jobs ∈ J had a chance to execute on n identical cores. It is easy to see that this problem is a variation of the n-dimensional bin-packing and thus NP-Hard [39].

Thus, an approximation is used. The earliest time a job ∈ J starts its execution is the earliest release time of any job ∈ J. Since there is no information about the applied scheduling algorithm at this early development phase, the execution of all jobs is approximated. It is assumed that each job may start its execution at the same time, and the complete workload can be parallelized over all available cores. Note that a job cannot be executing on two cores simultaneously. Hence, the minimum between the number of jobs |J| and the number of cores n is used as a divider for the sum of workloads:

1) Finding θ n pred : θ n pred can directly be obtained from θ n by observing that J = dep pred (τ i,j ). The execution starts earliest with the earliest release of any job in dep pred (τ i,j ). This gives the lower bound on the earliest time the workload of dep pred (τ i,j ) can be executed by any scheduling algorithm.
div.formula: θ n pred = min ∀τ B,k ∈J (R B,k ) + θ n(14)
div.p: 2) Finding θ n suc : In order to find an upper bound on the latest possible time the workloads in dep suc (τ i,j ) need to start executing it can be noticed that this is the inverse problem of finding θ n pred , i.e., the latest execution is of interest. Consequently, the maximum deadline of all jobs in dep suc (τ i,j ) is chosen and θ n is subtracted:
div.formula: θ n suc = max ∀τ B,k ∈J (D B,k ) -θ n(15)
div.p: The presented calculations reflect lower bounds on E Start i,j and E End i,j

and can thus be used to give a bound on the least number of cores required to schedule the system under the specified job-level dependencies. If additional system information is available, θ n pred and θ n suc can be refined to obtain tighter estimates, however the overall structure of the schedulability test remains the same.

div.head: IX. EVALUATION
div.p: This section evaluates the proposed method for the reaction delay computations presented in Section IV. Experiments based on synthetic task sets are performed to show the reduced pessimism in the calculations, as well as the impact of the effective input period which has been introduced for causeeffect chains with given reaction constraints.

Synthetic task sets are generated with 8 tasks in each set, where each set has a utilization of 50%. The periods of the tasks are chosen out of the set of periods commonly found in automotive applications [1,2,5,10,20,50,100,200, 1000] ms [2], and task utilizations are generated by UUniFast [40]. Response times of the tasks are calculated for systems with one CPU, with the assumption of fixed priority scheduling. Priorities are assigned based on the Rate Monotonic algorithm [13]. As the experiments target the data propagation delay all task sets are schedulable in terms of the tasks local deadlines. Each system contains a causeeffect chain which has a size of 2 to 5 tasks. For each setting 500 samples are collected and results are presented using boxplots.

div.head: A. Reduced Pessimism
div.p: Fig. 9a presents the results, comparing the original computation of [11] against the revised calculations. The improvement of the revised calculations with respect to the original calculations is shown in percent. The median values show that small chains of size 2 do not experience significant improvement, whereas the median improvement for longer cause-effect chains is around 40%. This shows that the revised calculations lead to significantly tighter results when longer chains are analyzed. Note that the reduced pessimism is contributed to the more accurate upper bound on ∆ Input presented in Section IV.

div.head: B. Effective Input Period
div.p: Fig. 9b depicts the ratio between the effective input period of the first task in a cause-effect chain and the input sampling delay of the chain as calculated in [11]. A value smaller than 1 states the ratio which the old input sampling delay is larger than the revised, safe, effective input period. The median values show a trend of decreasing ratio with increasing chain length. Hence, with increasing length of the chain, the introduced overapproximation of the input sampling delay is increasing as well.
This further highlights and reinforces our claim that system designers must take the effective input period of a chain into account instead of the period of the first task in the chain.

div.head: X. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: With increasing system complexity and demands on today's applications, the verification of specified data propagation delay constraints becomes intrinsically important already at early stages of system development. This early detection of design flaws has significant benefits, as design changes may be required (both for the required effort to address the change as for its financial implications).

In this paper, we have identified a source of unsafe bound as well as pessimism in the calculations of the reaction delay, one of the data propagation delays, in a state-of-the-art approach. The calculations are revised and a solution is proposed that corrects these unsafe bounds and leads to tighter results. Moreover, we have presented methods to compute upper bounds on all data propagation delay semantics of the data propagation through a chain of independently triggered tasks that communicate via register communication. Additionally, the system model is augmented with job-level dependencies, a partial execution order on task's jobs, such that the specified data propagation delay constraints are met. This is done by specifying all necessary dependencies and then, in a second step, removing the dependencies that are either implicitly warranted by other dependencies or by the system characteristics in general. A necessary schedulability test is also presented that takes the number of available CPUs into account but is otherwise agnostic of the applied scheduling algorithm. Thus, it can be applied at high abstraction levels and used for platform dimensioning. Finally, evaluations are performed that demonstrate the identified source of optimism and pessimism in the state-of-the-art and practice solutions. The importance for system designers to take the effective input period of a chain into account is highlighted by experiments.

Future work will target schedulability tests for multiprocessor systems that take different communication delays into account, that are experienced due to inter-task communication on the same core and on different cores.
